title: Tackling ML-based Dynamic Mispredictions using Statically Computed Invariants for Attack Surface Reduction
problem: ML-based runtime predictors used for code debloating and dynamic control flow monitoring lack guarantees that distinguish mispredictions from actual security attacks, making them unsuitable for safety-critical security contexts. Without this distinction, the system either blocks legitimate executions (false positives from mispredictions) or fails to stop real attacks.
motivation: The increasing adoption of ML for runtime control flow and security decisions creates a correctness-security gap: ML predictions are accurate but not guaranteed, yet security enforcement requires distinguishing false positives (ML error) from true positives (adversarial attack).
method: Before the program runs, the approach analyzes the code to identify behaviors that are definitely safe—these are called static invariants (unchanging properties proven to be secure). It removes these safe behaviors from what the ML-based predictor needs to check, shrinking the 'attack surface' (the set of actions that could be security risks). Now the ML predictor only makes predictions on genuinely ambiguous situations, so when it flags something as suspicious, it's much more likely to be an actual attack rather than a false alarm, making it safe to enforce security policies like control flow integrity (blocking unexpected code jumps) and debloating (removing unused code).
key_novelty: The core idea is using static analysis to identify definitely-safe program behaviors and exclude them from the ML predictor's evaluation, so the predictor operates only on genuinely risky situations where its predictions reliably distinguish attacks from false alarms.
contributions: Formulation of the misprediction-vs-attack disambiguation problem for ML-based runtime security monitors.
Static invariant computation approach to shrink the set of behaviors that the ML predictor must adjudicate.
Integration with debloating and control flow monitoring use cases to demonstrate attack surface reduction.
Evaluation showing improved precision of ML-based security decisions after invariant-guided reduction.
limitations: Quantitative results and specific static analysis techniques not available from abstract alone.
primary_theme: static invariants to bound ML-based security prediction errors
